summary: Describes DASS, the Distributed Authentication Security Service, an experimental design for proving who users and services are in a distributed environment, aiming to be both more secure and easier to use than existing mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: How do you prove who you are to a stranger far away. DASS is one plan for carrying a trustworthy ID card that works across many computers.

questions: how does dass use certification authorities
how does dass prevent replay attacks
subtitle: An experimental architecture for proving who users, servers and computers are across a network, using public keys and a hierarchy of certification authorities.

tldr.problem: Passwords can be eavesdropped on the network, and in a distributed system a user ends up with a separate account on every machine. The RFC wants authentication that is both more secure and easier to use.
tldr.mechanism: DASS gives each principal an RSA key pair and a certificate signed by a certification authority. Certification authorities form a hierarchy that follows the X.500 naming hierarchy. A claimant sends a timestamped authentication token, and the verifier checks certificates found in a naming service.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol. It also lays the groundwork for smart cards and for sharing one login across many machines, but the RFC itself does not report any deployment.

today: RFC 1507 is an Experimental protocol from September 1993, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself does not describe any deployment.

sections.title: What DASS Is For
sections.content:
The Distributed Authentication Security Service (DASS) provides authentication in a distributed environment that is both more secure and easier to use than password schemes. Authentication means reliably learning the name of the originator of a message or request. DASS aims at strong, mutual authentication: each party learns the other's name, and neither learns anything it could use to impersonate the other to a third party. Plain passwords cannot do this, because whoever speaks first reveals information the other side could reuse.

DASS also supports global identity and network login. A user gets one name from a global namespace that every node recognises, so a single password or smart card can be used on all systems, and the password never needs to appear on the network beyond the initial login node. DASS was designed as a component of the Distributed System Security Architecture (DSSA). The RFC suggests that databases such as .rhosts could be extended to grant access to local accounts based on DASS global names.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a different secret word for every clubhouse, you get one proof-of-who-you-are that all the clubhouses accept, and you never have to shout it across the playground.

sections.title: Central Concepts
sections.content:
DASS makes heavy use of the RSA public key cryptosystem. Each principal (a user or a computer) has a public/private key pair, publishes the public key and keeps the private key secret. A signature made with the private key can be checked by anyone with the public key.

To stop replay of a signed message, there are two standard methods: challenge/response, which always needs at least three messages, and timestamps, which need securely synchronized time and a server that remembers recent messages. DASS uses timestamps, so authentication messages can be piggybacked on existing connection setup and fit the same message pattern as Kerberos. As an example, the RFC says a server might reject messages older than, say, five minutes.

Delegation lets a login node, and optionally a server such as a remote login service, act for the user. A login node uses the user's secret while the user is logged in and forgets it at logout. This version limits delegation only in terms of time. DASS can also authenticate a user and a node together, so access control can depend on both. User private keys can be stored encrypted under a password, and an optional login agent can audit and limit password guessing.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone has a secret stamp that only they own, and a public picture of what its mark looks like. Stamping a note with the date shows it is fresh, so nobody can reuse an old note.

sections.title: Certificates and the CA Hierarchy
sections.content:
A certification authority (CA) is a principal that signs certificates stating a name, a public key and an expiration date. A single global CA would be a central point of trust, so DASS ties the CA hierarchy to the naming hierarchy. Each directory has one CA, which certifies its members, the CAs of child directories and the CA of the parent directory. Knowing the public key of any CA, a principal can walk the tree to verify any other. A compromised CA can only impersonate principals within its own part of the tree. DASS uses X.500 names for principals, and when parts of the tree have no CA it uses cross-certificates.

Certificates follow X.509 syntax but are treated as one of six types: normal principal, trusted authority, child, parent, cross and self. In the first five, the relationship of the issuer's name to the subject's name decides the type. Each certificate carries the issuer and subject names, the subject's public key, a validity period and a signature. Every certificate is expected to expire in about a year, and names in child and principal certificates are used only by suffix so that renaming a branch does not invalidate them.

DASS has two revocation mechanisms: certificate expiry, and removing the certificate from the naming service. It does not support X.509 revocation lists.
sections.plainLanguage: A school office makes ID cards, and each wing of the school has its own office. A teacher can check a card by walking up the chain of offices until one they already trust vouches for it.

sections.title: Authentication Tokens and Credentials
sections.content:
The claimant builds an authentication token with Create_token, and the target checks it with Accept_token. The token holds an encrypted shared DES key, protected with the target's public key, a login ticket, a shared key ticket, an optional node ticket and delegator, and an authenticator. The authenticator is a timestamp and a digest of channel bindings, protected with the shared key, and is always present. The login ticket is a delegation certificate signed by the principal's long-term private key, handing over to a short-term delegation key. This way the long-term key need not stay in the system.

With mutual authentication, the target answers with a much simpler token that contains only the timestamp from the authenticator, encrypted under the shared key.

A DASS implementation keeps its state in a single credentials structure with many optional fields. Claimant credentials let a process create tokens, verifier credentials let a server check them, and the RFC lists combined and stub forms as well. Credentials hold secrets, so the RFC expects an implementation to hand applications only a handle to them. DASS stores its certificates in a naming service, ideally X.500, and the RFC also describes an alternative certificate distribution center protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The note you hand over has your ID card, a sealed envelope only the receiver can open, and a fresh date stamp. The receiver stamps the date back to show they got it.

sections.title: The Exchange Step by Step
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the six phases of the OSI Authentication Framework. In installation, a CA enrols and validates a principal and issues a certificate. In distribution, certificates go into the name service. In acquisition, principals fetch certificates and build credentials, with the user holding a trusted authority for the CA. In transfer, the claimant sends its token. In verification, the verifier recovers the DES key, fetches certificates, and checks all signatures, keeping verified authenticators for a suitable timeout. Unenrolment removes information from the name service.

To make a token, the claimant first fetches the verifier's certificate from the name service (shown as a certificate distribution center, CDC, in the figure). The authenticator can only be used once, but the same authentication context can be re-established several times, so caching saves repeated public key operations.

The RFC also lists the services DASS needs: time accurate to within a few hours for certificate checks, time synchronized within a few minutes for replay detection, cryptographic-quality random numbers, and a highly available, timely naming service.
sections.plainLanguage: First you get your ID, then it is put on file, then you pick up the right forms, show your card at the door, and the door checks it with the office. When you leave, your name comes off the list.

sections.title: Trust, Time and Weak Points
sections.content:
The RFC's security section just says that security issues are discussed throughout the memo. The main discussion points are these.

Timestamps depend on clocks. If a client's clock is made fast enough that its tokens are rejected, someone harvesting those tokens could replay them later. Inaccurate time can also cause valid requests to be rejected or expired ones accepted. Expiry is a backup revocation mechanism, so a compromise would need multiple failures.

The security of DASS applications does not in general depend on the naming service, but two things do: timely revocation of certificates, and protection against dictionary guessing of passwords. If the naming service is not authenticated, as expected in early versions, a revoked certificate could be reinstated by impersonating it. Between the first link from a user to a DASS node and a smart card, the RFC admits that the first link remains vulnerable to eavesdropping.
sections.plainLanguage: The system works only if the clocks agree and the list of ID cards is guarded, so those are the places a sneaky person would try.
